This could be correct, but it is based on old papers and seems increasingly unlikely as the activity does not fit very well mechanistically (it's a tRNA hydrolase)

It would be better to propagate the human annotation:
rescue of stalled cytosolic ribosome
which is a better studied and conserved role for Cdc48p-Npl4p-Vms1p

(note that Cdc48p-Npl4p-Ufd1 is ERAD)

* Add the label 'high priority' if needed. Generally high priority issues affect a lot of proteins, and annotations are incorrect (as opposed to just imprecise).

Claude 
What Vms1 does, more precisely:

Its main, best-characterized job is RQC (ribosome rescue). Vms1 (ANKZF1 in mammals) is a peptidyl-tRNA hydrolase — its key enzymatic function is to cleave the bond linking a stalled nascent chain to its tRNA, freeing the polypeptide from the stuck 60S ribosomal subunit so Cdc48-Ufd1-Npl4 can pull it out and hand it to the proteasome. The Cdc48 adaptor Vms1 is a peptidyl-tRNA hydrolase that cooperates with the ribosome quality control complex to catalyse the removal of nascent polypeptides from stalled ribosomes. This is genuinely a distinct role from Ufd1-Npl4: Cdc48 extraction requires that the 60S-trapped nascent chain be released from the tRNA to which it is covalently linked, and Vms1 has been identified as the factor performing this function. 
[PubMed Central](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6226276/)
[PubMed Central](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7138134/)
But yeast Vms1 also contributes directly to ERAD, at a step downstream of ubiquitination — Vms1 is a component of a Cdc48p-complex involved in protein quality control, and contributes to ER-associated degradation (ERAD) of specific substrates at a step after their ubiquitination. It binds Cdc48 directly through its own binding motif: Vms1 binds the N-terminal domain of Cdc48 via its VIM domain, alongside the canonical Ufd1-Npl4 ERAD cofactors. 
[SGD](https://www.yeastgenome.org/locus/S000002456)
[ScienceDirect](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167488911002606)
Vms1 also has a third role, in mitochondria-associated degradation (MAD) — it translocates to mitochondria under oxidative stress and forms a complex with Cdc48p and Npl4p required for ubiquitin-mediated mitochondria-associated protein degradation. 
[BioGRID](https://thebiogrid.org/32103/summary/saccharomyces-cerevisiae/vms1.html)

So the honest answer to "is Vms1 involved in ERAD" is: yes, at least in yeast, though it's a minor/accessory player there compared to Ufd1-Npl4, which are the core ERAD adaptors. Vms1's dominant, mechanistically well-defined role is ribosome rescue (RQC), but it isn't ERAD-exclusive — it's really a multi-purpose Cdc48 cofactor (RQC, ERAD, and mitochondrial protein degradation), which is probably exactly why your source lumped "ribosome rescue/ERAD branch" together under the same complex name rather than treating them as fully separate pathways.
